title: Migration, Labour Mobility and Industrial Skills

Migration, Labour Mobility and Industrial Skills

# Migration, Labour Mobility and Industrial Skills

About a fifth of manufacturing workers in England and Wales were born abroad in 2021: 40% in food, 12% to 20% in engineering. Sponsored work visas to manufacturers are down by more than half from their 2024 peak, while rules tightened.

Published, revised

Updated

21 October 2026

Two questions sit under this article. How much have migrants added to the skills British factories use? And what have changes to the immigration rules done to manufacturers? The first can now be answered with numbers for England and Wales. The second can be answered only in part, because the figures that exist show what happened to visas and not what happened to factories.

The short answer is that manufacturing as a whole relies on workers born abroad about as much as the economy as a whole does, and the engineering trades less so. Reliance is greatest in food processing and in production-line jobs, which sponsored visas have largely not covered since 2021. Since then sponsored visas have been a small fraction of the manufacturing workforce, and they have fallen sharply since 2024. Whether that has cost output, delayed projects or pushed firms to train more is not something any source we found measures.

## How Much of Manufacturing Rests on Workers Born Abroad

The 2021 Census counted 2,040,217 people in England and Wales whose job was in manufacturing. Of these, 21.3% were born outside the UK, against 20.9% across all industries. 1 About 12.1% of manufacturing workers were born in an EU country (Ireland included) and 9.2% elsewhere in the world.

The average hides a sharp divide. In food products, 40.4% of the 295,000 workers were born abroad; in clothing the share was 40.1%. In machinery and equipment it was 13.3%, in other transport equipment (which includes aerospace) 12.0% and in repair and installation of machinery 10.7%. Across the six engineering divisions, from fabricated metal products to other transport equipment, the shares ran from 12.0% to 19.5%. 1 Food factories hold 14.5% of manufacturing jobs but 27.4% of its workers born abroad; without them the manufacturing share is 18.1%.

The pattern holds by occupation across all industries. Of people working in metal forming, welding and related trades, 12.7% were born abroad; the shares were 12.0% in metal machining, fitting and instrument making, 12.4% in electrical and electronic trades and 19.7% among engineering professionals. For process operatives, the people who run production lines, it was 41.5%, and for all occupations 20.9%. 2 The Migration Advisory Committee’s (MAC) nationality-based estimates agree: in 2022 to 2024, 92% of engineering technicians, 90% of metal working production and maintenance fitters and 85% of welders were UK nationals. 3 

These figures call for care. Country of birth is not nationality, and the Census count includes British citizens born abroad as well as people who arrived as children and were trained here. The Census was taken in March 2021 and covers England and Wales only. Nor does a snapshot say whether reliance has grown or shrunk. In the sources we reviewed there is no published series of the foreign-born share of manufacturing jobs over time.

What the snapshot does show is that migration is not what staffs Britain’s engineering trades: they are overwhelmingly filled by people born here. Migration matters most for lower-skilled production work, and for particular professional and technical roles that the visa figures below point to.

## What Free Movement Added and Its End Removed

Until the end of 2020 EU citizens could take any job in Britain without sponsorship. The new points-based system introduced in January 2021 lowered salary and skill requirements for non-EU citizens but was far more restrictive for EU citizens, who had previously enjoyed full access to the labour market. Common low-wage roles such as food processing labourers were not eligible for work visas. 4 For manufacturing the effect was uneven. Portes and Springford compared employment in mid-2022 with what pre-pandemic trends would have implied. They estimated 277,000 EU-origin workers in manufacturing against a counterfactual of 324,000, a shortfall of 47,000, and 234,000 non-EU workers against 242,000, a shortfall of 7,900. They found no visible substitution of non-EU for EU workers in manufacturing, and very few work visas issued to the sector. 5 In our arithmetic the combined shortfall is about 55,000 workers, or 9.7% of the counterfactual non-UK-origin manufacturing workforce.

The authors warn that it is very difficult to separate changes caused by labour supply from changes caused by labour demand, and the counterfactual simply extends pre-pandemic trends. The Migration Observatory reached a similar verdict from a wider base: immigration policy was one of multiple factors behind labour shortages, alongside tight post-pandemic labour markets in countries that had not changed their rules and long-standing problems of pay and conditions. 4 Its review of employer responses found qualitative evidence that food and drink manufacturers were automating more processes, though automation was limited by the cost of initial investment, and no widespread pay rises in industries that had relied on EU workers by mid-2022. 4 

More recent data show the eastern European workforce shrinking gradually. Employee jobs held by adult nationals of the eight eastern European states that joined in 2004 (the EU8) fell 16% between January 2021 and December 2025 and those of Bulgaria and Romania (the EU2) fell 7%. Just over a third of the EU8 jobs were in retail or manufacturing. 6 Those figures cover employees by nationality, not birthplace, and exclude the self-employed.

## The Rules Have Tightened Twice

Two changes matter for manufacturers. In April 2024 the government replaced the Shortage Occupation List with a narrower Immigration Salary List, abolished the 20% discount on the going rate and raised the general salary threshold for the Skilled Worker route from £26,200 to £38,700, with occupation-specific thresholds raised to the median full-time salary. 7 The 2025 white paper said these increases had reduced visas at every skill level. 8 

The second change came into force on 22 July 2025. The government lifted the skill threshold back to level 6 of the Regulated Qualifications Framework (RQF), the graduate level, removing around 180 occupations from the main route. 9 3 Skilled Worker applicants in jobs below that level can be sponsored only if they were already in the route, or if the occupation sits on an interim Immigration Salary List or a new interim Temporary Shortage List. New workers in those jobs cannot bring dependants, and both lists have removal dates at the end of 2026. 9 The white paper made the temporary list conditional on MAC advice, a workforce strategy and a commitment by employers to recruit more from the domestic workforce, and announced a 32% rise in the Immigration Skills Charge, the first since 2017. 8 

The rules as updated on 8 October 2026 set a general salary requirement of £41,700, or £33,400 for a job on the Immigration Salary List. The interim Temporary Shortage List covers 3112 electrical and electronics technicians, 3113 engineering technicians, 3116 planning, process and production technicians, 5213 welding trades and 5223 metal working production and maintenance fitters among others, but only for certificates of sponsorship issued before 31 December 2026. It does not include 5211 sheet metal workers or 5221 metal machining setters and setter-operators. 10 

In July 2026 the MAC reviewed 82 occupations that might qualify for the Temporary Shortage List. It recommended 18-month access for 28 and none for the full three years; within Advanced Manufacturing it put welding at the stronger end and metal working fitters at the weaker. 3 The 82 occupations accounted for about 10,000 visas a year on average from 2022/23 to 2024/25, and the 28 recommended for about 4,000, so the MAC expected “a relatively small reduction in migration”. It had earlier recommended that salary thresholds on the list be set at the median full-time earnings of each occupation, so that a migrant must be paid at least what the median worker in that job earns. 3 We found no published government decision on these recommendations at 21 October 2026, and the rules of 8 October still carry the interim lists. 10 

## What Has Happened to Visas for Manufacturers

The Home Office publishes entry clearance grants to people applying from outside the UK, by the industry the sponsor chose and by occupation. For manufacturing sponsors, grants on the Skilled Worker route rose from 4,168 in the year to June 2022 to a peak of 7,272 in the year to June 2024, then fell to 3,191 and 2,307 in the next two years, a fall of 68% from the peak. All sponsored work routes together fell 58%, from 9,245 to 3,917. 11

Set against the workforce the numbers are small. At the 2024 peak, Skilled Worker grants to manufacturing sponsors equalled 0.29% of UK manufacturing workforce jobs; in the year to June 2026 they equalled 0.09%. 11 12 Manufacturing sponsors took 8.6% of all Skilled Worker grants in the latest year and 3.7% of all sponsored work grants. Another route, Senior or Specialist Worker for intra-company transfers, accounted for 1,409 manufacturing grants in the year to June 2026, more than half as many as the Skilled Worker route. 11
